newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's unemployment rises to 9.6 pct in April.
newsitem.headline: Canada's unemployment rises to 9.6 pct in April.

text.p: Statistics Canada, in its last such release before the June 2 federal election, said on Friday the unemployment rate rose to 9.6 percent in April from 9.3 percent in March.
Note - Labor force, employment and unemployment in millions, on seasonally adjusted basis.
A Reuters survey of economists had forecast the unemployment rate to remain unchanged.
Full-time employment rose by 41,100 from the month before, mostly among the self-employed, while part-time employment fell by 7,800.
A Reuters survey of economists had forecast employment to grow by 38,600.
Since last September, when employment growth resumed after a summer of little overall change, employment has increased by an estimated 166,000, Statistics Canada said.

But April's employment growth was accompanied by a large increase of 79,000 in the labor force. When unemployment rates rise, Finance Minister Paul Martin tends to point to a larger labor force as a sign of confidence in the economy.

The employment growth was all among adults (40,000). Adult women accounted for 24,000 of this growth, nearly all of it full time. Since September adult men have added 119,000 jobs and adult women 69,000.
But the situation was bleaker for youth aged 15-24. Their unemployment rate rose 0.4 points to 17.0 percent.
"Despite a large decline in labor force participation during the 1990s, difficult labor market conditions for youth have kept their unemployment rate high," Statistics Canada said.

Employment gains in April were mainly in construction (+ 17,000) and transportation, storage and communication (+ 13,000). Employment was little changed in manufacturing and trade, following significant gains during the previous month.

Private sector employment grew by 37,000 in April, with the gain concentrated among the self-employed (+24,000). Public sector employment showed little change on the month but was 60,000 down from a year earlier.

Statistics Canada said its employment number should have a margin of error of 62,000 95 percent of the time, or 32,000 67 percent of the time. Its unemployment number should have a margin of error of 46,000 95 percent of the time or 24,000 67 percent of the time.
